Daily Transit Intelligence
June 21, 2026 — 12 papers analyzed
KEY FINDINGS
A slime-mold-inspired demand-responsive bus swarm increased passenger
delivery 28–101% and cut walking time over 75% versus fixed routes.
Free bus fares for women across five Indian states raised paid-work
participation, with the largest gains in the most mobility-restricted,
patriarchal districts.
NYC's congestion pricing lifted bus and subway ridership well beyond the
tolled zone, while its travel-demand reduction stayed concentrated inside
it — an uneven distribution of costs and benefits.
PAPER OF THE DAY
A Swarm Approach to Public Transit Using On-demand Routing in a
Slime-Mold-Inspired Framework
Lindsay Burke, Maxfield Comstock, Jason Graham, Ruth Malenda, Simon Garnier, Petras Swissler
A demand-responsive transit swarm that routes buses using a slime-mold-inspired cooperative
bidding algorithm increases passenger delivery rates by 28–101% over fixed-route networks
and cuts walking time by more than 75% across suburban, urban, and semi-rural simulations.
Why it matters: it shows decentralized, biologically-inspired control can beat both fixed routes
and centrally-scheduled demand-responsive transit without adding fleet size.
EMERGING THEMES
Bio-inspired and AI-driven
routing converges on adaptive,
decentralized coordination
Equity research shifts from
describing disparities to
prescribing fare/access levers
Trip planning and network
science scale toward unified,
continental-size toolkits
CONFIDENCE DISTRIBUTION
High
Medium
Low
ACTIONABLE TAKEAWAYS
Agencies exploring demand-responsive transit in low-density areas should pilot decentralized,
swarm-style dynamic routing rather than centralized dispatch.
Cities weighing fare policy as an equity lever should test free or steeply discounted fares for
specific demographics before assuming broad fare-capping is most efficient.
Trip-planning teams should benchmark continental-scale algorithms like T-REX before accepting
multi-second query times as inevitable on dense networks.
15-minute-city planners should treat transit access and active-mobility access as complementary,
not substitutable, since transit lines alone don't equalize peripheral amenity access.
Teams piloting LLM trip planners should combine fine-tuning with retrieval-augmented generation,
since each method alone leaves accuracy gaps the other fills.
